title: Atlas: hypervised desktop for autonomous agents
excerpt: Atlas gives your agent a hidden, signed-in macOS desktop where it uses apps, clicks, types and takes screenshots, while you keep using your Mac.
content_html:
hypervised desktop
for autonomous agents

Atlas gives your agent a hidden second desktop on your Mac. It opens apps, clicks and types there while you keep working on yours.

curl -fsSL https://atlas.insanearts.io/install.sh | sh

Inside the harness.

Your agent’s desktop, in the tools you already use. Pick a harness and try a task.

“Find a free hour on Thursday afternoon and add a launch review to my calendar.”

Connect your harness in Atlas → Settings → Agents.

Set up once.
Then it's your agent's Mac.

  1. 1

    Install once.

    One command, then the usual macOS prompts. Atlas sets up a hidden desktop on your Mac.

  2. 2

    You keep working.

    Ask your agent for something and get back to your work. Your screen, mouse and keyboard stay yours.

  3. 3

    Watch it work.

    Open Atlas to see your agent on its own desktop, clicking through your app and taking screenshots.

Bring what the task needs. Atlas can copy a build, sample files or settings into the helper, then clean up after the task.

Ask in plain language. Your agent opens apps, clicks controls by name, types and brings back screenshots.

Less context, same work.

Every screenshot and every page of instructions fills your agent’s context. Here is what the same three tasks took through Atlas and through each agent’s own Computer Use, on the same model.

  • ClaudeClaude Opus 5.5

    6.4×less context with Atlas

    Atlas36k

    Computer Use232k

    Tokens by taskAtlasComputer Use
    Write and save a TextEdit document9.5k37k
    Turn on three TextEdit settings14k25k
    Fill and submit a web form in Chrome13k170k

    Screenshots a task
    1.7vs 54.5

    Time a task
    41 svs 203 s

    Tasks finished
    9 of 9vs 8 of 9

    Computer Use looks at the whole screen after every step, so a form with five fields took up to 153 screenshots.

  • CodexGPT-6.1 Sol, medium

    1.4×less context with Atlas

    Atlas20k

    Computer Use28k

    Tokens by taskAtlasComputer Use
    Write and save a TextEdit document5.2k9.3k
    Turn on three TextEdit settings8.1k11k
    Fill and submit a web form in Chrome6.3k7.9k

    Screenshots a task
    1.7vs 0

    Time a task
    36 svs 30 s

    Tasks finished
    9 of 9vs 9 of 9

    Codex’s Computer Use reads apps as text, so it took no screenshots and finished a little sooner. With Atlas, Codex took about two a task. Most of the context gap is instructions: about 6k tokens, against 2k for Atlas.

Tokens of context each task added, median of three runs, on a MacBook Pro. Claude: Claude Code with Atlas, and Anthropic’s computer-use tool (computer_toolset_20260801, set up as its documentation describes) driving the same apps in the same helper. Codex: Codex with Atlas, and Codex’s own Computer Use on the desktop. Tokenizers differ, so each card has its own scale: compare bars within a card, not across them. A computer-use loop that takes fewer screenshots would cost less.

Quiet until there’s work.

The helper is a real macOS login on your Mac. Here is how it shares your Mac, and what it costs.

  1. Idle means idle.

    When your agent finishes, it quits every app it opened and leaves the helper quiet, so nothing sits in memory for no reason. Until the next task, Atlas does nothing.

  2. One at a time.

    Agents queue for the helper: one acts, the others are told Atlas is busy and wait their turn. Take Control puts you ahead of all of them.

  3. You set the cost.

    So it never drains your battery for nothing: watch live, every 5 seconds or paused, Stop holds every agent, atlas close --all quits what they opened and atlas logout signs the helper out.

Questions, answered.

A second macOS login on your Mac, signed in and running in the background. It is your agent’s desktop: its own windows, menu bar, Dock, settings and files. You stay in your own account and never see it unless you open Atlas.

No. The helper is an ordinary macOS account on the same Mac, so apps run at full speed with no image to download or keep in sync. It shares your Mac’s hardware, network and speakers. It is not a security sandbox: give agents the same trust you would give them in a terminal.

No. Agents act only in the helper, through its own input service. There is no fallback to your screen. If the helper ever comes on screen, Atlas refuses to act until you switch back.

Computer Use works on your own screen: it brings windows up in front of you, you can’t keep working while it runs, and it takes over your screen, which hurts most on a small one. With Atlas the agent does all of that on its own hidden desktop, and your windows, keyboard and mouse stay yours.

Anything that needs a screen: open your build and check it in Dark mode, sign up on your local web app in Chrome, reproduce a bug someone describes, run an installer or a first launch, use Calendar, Notes or System Settings, and bring back screenshots of each step.

They take turns. Only one controller acts on the helper at a time; another agent is told Atlas is busy and waits. When you choose Take Control, your mouse and keyboard come first until you give it back.

Yes. Stop, in the menu bar or the viewer, cancels input underway and refuses every further agent action until you choose Resume. Agents can’t resume themselves.

Claude, Codex, Cursor, opencode and Pi. Claude works two ways: in the Claude app Atlas’s live view opens right in the chat, and in Claude Code /atlas-screen shows it. Codex and Cursor also show it in the chat; Cursor’s Agent CLI, opencode and Pi open Atlas’s own window. Connect them in Atlas’s Settings → Agents, or with atlas agents install.

The helper starts without them. An agent copies in only what a task needs, such as a build or a sample file, and rolls it back afterwards. Credentials and keychains are never copied, and nothing is copied back to your account.

Not from Atlas. It has no telemetry or analytics, and it goes online only to install and for atlas update, which download from atlas.insanearts.io. Screenshots stay on your Mac; when your agent reads one, it goes to the agent’s model like any other file it reads.

Native Save and Open panels and Safari’s web views need a connected Screen Sharing session; Chrome and Firefox work without one. Drag and drop of files onto apps isn’t supported. The helper’s sound plays on your speakers.

Yes. Atlas is free and open source under the MIT license, and its code is on GitHub.

A Mac with macOS 14 or later and an administrator account for setup. Setup creates the helper account, or uses one you choose, and you sign in to it once to allow Atlas.

atlas update installs the latest release after checking its signature. atlas uninstall removes Atlas and keeps the helper account, which you can delete in System Settings.

Give your agents
a Mac of their own.

Install Atlas once. Your agent takes it from there.

curl -fsSL https://atlas.insanearts.io/install.sh | sh

Read the docsStar Atlas on GitHub

content_html_zh:
hypervised desktopfor autonomous agents

Atlas gives your agent a hidden second desktop on your Mac. It opens apps, clicks and types there while you keep working on yours.

curl -fsSL https://atlas.insanearts.io/install.sh | sh

Inside the harness.

Your agent’s desktop, in the tools you already use. Pick a harness and try a task.

“Find a free hour on Thursday afternoon and add a launch review to my calendar.”

Connect your harness in Atlas → Settings → Agents.

Set up once.Then it's your agent's Mac.

  1. 1Install once.One command, then the usual macOS prompts. Atlas sets up a hidden desktop on your Mac.
  2. 2You keep working.Ask your agent for something and get back to your work. Your screen, mouse and keyboard stay yours.
  3. 3Watch it work.Open Atlas to see your agent on its own desktop, clicking through your app and taking screenshots.

Bring what the task needs. Atlas can copy a build, sample files or settings into the helper, then clean up after the task.

Ask in plain language. Your agent opens apps, clicks controls by name, types and brings back screenshots.

Less context, same work.

Every screenshot and every page of instructions fills your agent’s context. Here is what the same three tasks took through Atlas and through each agent’s own Computer Use, on the same model.

  • ClaudeClaude Opus 5.56.4×less context with AtlasAtlas36kComputer Use232kTokens by taskAtlasComputer UseWrite and save a TextEdit document9.5k37kTurn on three TextEdit settings14k25kFill and submit a web form in Chrome13k170kScreenshots a task1.7vs 54.5Time a task41 svs 203 sTasks finished9 of 9vs 8 of 9Computer Use looks at the whole screen after every step, so a form with five fields took up to 153 screenshots.
  • CodexGPT-6.1 Sol, medium1.4×less context with AtlasAtlas20kComputer Use28kTokens by taskAtlasComputer UseWrite and save a TextEdit document5.2k9.3kTurn on three TextEdit settings8.1k11kFill and submit a web form in Chrome6.3k7.9kScreenshots a task1.7vs 0Time a task36 svs 30 sTasks finished9 of 9vs 9 of 9Codex’s Computer Use reads apps as text, so it took no screenshots and finished a little sooner. With Atlas, Codex took about two a task. Most of the context gap is instructions: about 6k tokens, against 2k for Atlas.

Tokens of context each task added, median of three runs, on a MacBook Pro. Claude: Claude Code with Atlas, and Anthropic’s computer-use tool (computer_toolset_20260801, set up as its documentation describes) driving the same apps in the same helper. Codex: Codex with Atlas, and Codex’s own Computer Use on the desktop. Tokenizers differ, so each card has its own scale: compare bars within a card, not across them. A computer-use loop that takes fewer screenshots would cost less.

Quiet until there’s work.

The helper is a real macOS login on your Mac. Here is how it shares your Mac, and what it costs.

  1. Idle means idle.When your agent finishes, it quits every app it opened and leaves the helper quiet, so nothing sits in memory for no reason. Until the next task, Atlas does nothing.
  2. One at a time.Agents queue for the helper: one acts, the others are told Atlas is busy and wait their turn. Take Control puts you ahead of all of them.
  3. You set the cost.So it never drains your battery for nothing: watch live, every 5 seconds or paused, Stop holds every agent, atlas close --all quits what they opened and atlas logout signs the helper out.

A second macOS login on your Mac, signed in and running in the background. It is your agent’s desktop: its own windows, menu bar, Dock, settings and files. You stay in your own account and never see it unless you open Atlas.

No. The helper is an ordinary macOS account on the same Mac, so apps run at full speed with no image to download or keep in sync. It shares your Mac’s hardware, network and speakers. It is not a security sandbox: give agents the same trust you would give them in a terminal.

No. Agents act only in the helper, through its own input service. There is no fallback to your screen. If the helper ever comes on screen, Atlas refuses to act until you switch back.

Computer Use works on your own screen: it brings windows up in front of you, you can’t keep working while it runs, and it takes over your screen, which hurts most on a small one. With Atlas the agent does all of that on its own hidden desktop, and your windows, keyboard and mouse stay yours.

Anything that needs a screen: open your build and check it in Dark mode, sign up on your local web app in Chrome, reproduce a bug someone describes, run an installer or a first launch, use Calendar, Notes or System Settings, and bring back screenshots of each step.

They take turns. Only one controller acts on the helper at a time; another agent is told Atlas is busy and waits. When you choose Take Control, your mouse and keyboard come first until you give it back.
